rag.description: SendUser32KeyboardKey sends keys and shortcuts to native Windows applications through the User32 API. Keys come from the Key parameter or the Argument, so values can be built at run time. Sticky mode holds keys for shortcuts, and delays and layout selection keep keyboard automation reliable.

qa.question: What does SendUser32KeyboardKey do?
qa.answer: It sends one or more keyboard keys to the active native Windows application through the User32 API.

qa.question: Which parameters does SendUser32KeyboardKey support?
qa.answer: Key (repeatable key name), Delay (pause between keys), Sticky (hold keys together), and KeyboardLayout (en-US or he-IL).

qa.question: What does SendUser32KeyboardKey need to run?
qa.answer: A User32-compatible UIA driver session on Windows; with any other driver it returns without sending keys. Documentation: https://github.com/g4-api/g4-plugins/blob/main/docs/Actions/SendUser32KeyboardKey.md Source: https://github.com/g4-api/g4-plugins/blob/main/src/G4.Plugins.Ui/Actions.User32/SendUser32KeyboardKey.cs

qa.question: How do I send a plain letter key without Shift?
qa.answer: Use the lowercase letter, such as --Key:c, because an uppercase letter without Sticky is sent as Shift plus the letter.

qa.question: How is a SendUser32KeyboardKey rule defined?
qa.answer: Use pluginName SendUser32KeyboardKey with a single key name as the argument, or with an expression such as {{$ --Key:Ctrl --Key:C --Sticky}}.

qa.question: What is the SendUser32KeyboardKey manifest version and author?
qa.answer: The manifest version is 4 and the author is Roei Sabag.

qa.question: How does the SendUser32KeyboardKey manifest summarize the plugin?
qa.answer: It sends keyboard keys and shortcuts to native Windows applications, in sequence or held together with Sticky, with configurable delays and layouts.

qa.question: What happens when a key name is not recognized?
qa.answer: No error is reported: without Sticky nothing is sent, and with Sticky an invalid scan code is sent for that key.

description: ### Purpose
Sends keyboard keys and shortcuts to the active native Windows application through the User32 API.
It drives native or legacy applications that cannot be controlled through standard WebDriver keyboard input.
### Key Features and Functionality
| Feature                    | Description                                                                    |
| Native Application Support | Sends hardware scan codes to the active native Windows application.            |
| Multi-Key Sequences        | Repeats the `Key` parameter to press several keys in order.                    |
| Sticky Mode                | Holds all keys down together and releases them in reverse order for shortcuts. |
| Configurable Delay         | Sets the pause between keys; a value of 0 uses 100 milliseconds.               |
| Keyboard Layout Selection  | Switches between the `en-US` and `he-IL` layouts before sending keys.          |
| Alternate Key Names        | Accepts common spellings such as `Delete`, `PageDown`, and `Space`.            |
### Usages in RPA
| Use Case              | Description                                                                                   |
| Native App Automation | Drives native application menus, dialogs, and commands with keyboard shortcuts.               |
| Legacy Systems        | Automates legacy applications that cannot be driven through standard WebDriver keyboard APIs. |
### Usages in Automation Testing
| Use Case                     | Description                                                                                     |
| Keyboard Interaction Testing | Verifies keyboard-driven behavior of native applications with operating-system-level key input. |
| Shortcut Coverage            | Tests shortcuts and modifier combinations that standard WebDriver keyboard input cannot reach.  |
### Limitations
An unknown key name is not reported as an error: without `Sticky` it sends nothing, and with `Sticky` it sends an invalid scan code.

edge_cases: A non-User32 driver returns without sending the key
An empty Argument sends no key
An unknown key name sends nothing without Sticky
annotations.expected_result: The F5 key is sent to the active native application window, triggering its F5 action such as a refresh.
annotations.notes: Without a parameter expression, the Argument value is sent as one key name. It is the simplest form of the plugin.

description: ### Single key press via plain Argument
Send a single `F5` key press to the active native application window.
The key name is passed directly as the Argument value without any parameter expression, making this the simplest form of the plugin.

edge_cases: A non-User32 driver returns without sending keys
An unknown key name sends an invalid scan code with Sticky
Sticky with a single key behaves like a normal key press
annotations.expected_result: Ctrl and C are held down together and then released, sending the copy shortcut to the active native window.
annotations.notes: Sticky presses the keys in order, holds them, and releases them in reverse order. Use it for any shortcut that needs a modifier key held down.

description: ### Sticky keyboard shortcut — Ctrl+C
Simulate pressing `Ctrl + C` simultaneously using sticky mode to send the copy shortcut to the active native application.
The `--Sticky` switch holds both keys down and then releases them in reverse order, which modifier-key combinations require.

edge_cases: A Delay of 0 still waits 100 milliseconds between keys
A non-User32 driver returns without sending keys
Repeating the same key name sends it once per occurrence
annotations.expected_result: The Tab key is pressed three times with 300 milliseconds between presses, moving focus across three fields.
annotations.notes: Without Sticky, each key is pressed and released on its own in the order given. Repeat --Key to build a sequence of any length.

description: ### Sequential Tab key presses with delay
Simulate pressing the `Tab` key three times in sequence with a 300-millisecond delay between each press to navigate through input fields in a native application form.
In non-sticky mode each key is pressed and released individually in the order specified.

edge_cases: A non-User32 driver returns without sending keys
Latin letter names are not mapped in the he-IL layout
The he-IL layout must be installed on the machine
annotations.expected_result: The driver switches the input language to Hebrew Standard, then Alt and Shift are pressed together, which toggles to the next installed input language.
annotations.notes: KeyboardLayout switches the input language before any key is sent and selects the he-IL key map. Alt+Shift then uses the Windows shortcut for changing the input language.

description: ### Sticky input language switch — Alt+Shift with the Hebrew layout
Select the `he-IL` layout and press `Alt + Shift` together with `Sticky`.
The driver switches to the Hebrew layout first, and Alt+Shift then toggles to the next installed input language.

edge_cases: A non-User32 driver returns without sending keys
Shift is sent as the Left Shift key
System shortcuts such as Ctrl+Shift+Esc are handled by Windows before the application
annotations.expected_result: Ctrl, Shift, and Esc are held down together and then released in reverse order, opening the Windows Task Manager.
annotations.notes: Three-key Sticky combinations follow the same pattern as two-key shortcuts. All keys are held together regardless of how many Key parameters are given.

description: ### Three-key sticky combination — Ctrl+Shift+Esc
Simulate pressing `Ctrl + Shift + Esc` simultaneously using sticky mode to open the Windows Task Manager.
All three keys are held down and then released in reverse order, which this system-level keyboard shortcut requires.
Sets the pause between keys in milliseconds, given as a number or a time string such as `00:00:00.300`.
A value of `0`, the default, uses the driver minimum of 100 milliseconds between keys.
With `Sticky`, the pause applies between key presses, and the keys are then released without a pause.
Increase it when the target application needs more time to process each key.
parameters.name: Delay

description: Names one key to press, such as `Enter`, `Ctrl`, or `F5`; repeat the parameter to send several keys in order.
When the parameter is omitted, the rule `Argument` value is used as a single key name.
Common alternate spellings, such as `Delete`, `PageDown`, or `Space`, are accepted and converted before sending.
Without `Sticky`, an uppercase letter is sent as Shift plus that letter, so use a lowercase letter for a plain key press.

parameters.name: Sticky

description: Sets the keyboard layout used to switch the system input language and map key names to scan codes.
Use `en-US` for English keys and `he-IL` for the Hebrew Standard layout; the default is `en-US`.
The `he-IL` layout maps Hebrew letters instead of Latin letters and sends `/`, `'`, `,`, `.`, `[`, and `]` through different physical keys.
The driver switches to the selected layout before it sends any key.
parameters.name: KeyboardLayout

description: Selects the English (United States) keyboard layout.
It is used when the parameter is omitted.
values.name: en-US

description: Selects the Hebrew Standard keyboard layout.
Latin letter names are not mapped in this layout, so use the Hebrew letters or switch to `en-US` for them.
values.name: he-IL

description: Carries the `{{$ --Key:Name}}` parameter expression or a single key name to send through the User32 API.
When no parameter expression is used, the raw Argument value is sent as one key name.
Use the expression form to send several keys or to set `Sticky`, `Delay`, or `KeyboardLayout`.
properties.name: Argument

summary: Sends keyboard keys and shortcuts to native Windows applications through the User32 API.
Presses keys in sequence or holds them together with `Sticky` for shortcuts such as `Ctrl+C`.
Supports configurable delays and the `en-US` and `he-IL` keyboard layouts for reliable keyboard automation.
